complexity.name: Heap file: search on a key field
complexity.notes: A search on a non-key field always reads all b blocks, since any block may hold a match.

complexity.name: Heap file: insertion
complexity.average: O(1): read and rewrite the last block
complexity.notes: Deletion first has to find the record, so it costs as much as a search.

complexity.name: Sorted file: search on the ordering field
complexity.notes: Insertion must keep the order, rewriting about b/2 blocks on average unless an overflow area is used.

complexity.name: Static hash file: equality search
complexity.worst: b, if every record hashes to one bucket
complexity.notes: Range queries and searches on other fields still need a full scan.

complexity.name: Extendible hashing: equality search
complexity.best: 1 access with the directory in memory
complexity.notes: Growth splits one bucket at a time; the directory doubles only when the overflowing bucket's local depth equals the global depth.

complexity.name: Single-level index: search
complexity.notes: Binary search over the bᵢ index blocks, then one access to the data block.

complexity.name: Multilevel index: search
complexity.notes: One block per index level, then the data block.

complexity.name: B-tree: search
complexity.best: 1 node, when the key is in the root
complexity.notes: A search may stop at an internal node, but most keys sit on the lowest level, so the average is close to h.

complexity.name: B+ tree: point search
complexity.notes: Every search ends at a leaf; add 1 to read the data block when the leaves hold record pointers.

complexity.name: B+ tree: insertion
complexity.worst: O(h) writes when splits reach the root
complexity.notes: Splits are rare when nodes are large, and even a cascade up to the root keeps the cost O(log_p n).

complexity.name: B+ tree: range query
complexity.best: h node reads when the range fits in one leaf
complexity.average: h + L − 1 node reads for L leaves in the range
complexity.notes: One root-to-leaf search finds the first key, and the linked leaves are then read in key order. An unclustered index adds one data-block access per matching record.

problemTypes.title: Block accesses with and without an index
recipe: Compute the blocking factor bfr = ⌊B / R⌋ and the data blocks b = ⌈r / bfr⌉.
Count index entries: one per data block for a primary index, one per record for a secondary index on a key. Divide by fo = ⌊B / (K + P)⌋ to get the index blocks bᵢ.
Single level: ⌈log₂ bᵢ⌉ + 1 accesses. Multilevel: divide by fo repeatedly until one block remains, and add 1 for the data block to the number of levels.
problemTypes.trap: Giving a primary index one entry per record instead of one per block, or forgetting the final data-block access.

problemTypes.title: Order of a B-tree or B+ tree node from block size
recipe: List what the node holds: keys, child pointers and, for B-tree nodes and B+ tree leaves, record pointers.
Set up the inequality: internal B+ node nK + (n + 1)P ≤ B; leaf n(K + Pr) + P ≤ B; B-tree node n(K + Pr) + (n + 1)P ≤ B.
Take the largest integer n, and report keys or children according to how the question defines order.
problemTypes.trap: Adding record pointers to a B+ tree internal node, or giving the key count when the question asks for the number of children.

problemTypes.title: Maximum or minimum keys and nodes for a given height
recipe: For the maximum, fill every node: level j has m^(j−1) nodes, each with m − 1 keys in a B-tree, and B+ tree leaves hold the leaf capacity.
For the minimum, give the root 2 children and every other node ⌈m/2⌉ children, with the minimum number of keys in each node.
Add up level by level, or use m^L − 1 and 2⌈m/2⌉^(L−1) − 1 for a B-tree.
problemTypes.trap: Applying the ⌈m/2⌉ minimum to the root, or counting levels from 0 when the question counts the root as level 1.

problemTypes.title: Trace insertions with node splits
recipe: Insert each key into its leaf in sorted order, and split only when the node exceeds its maximum.
On a B+ tree leaf split, copy the first key of the new right leaf into the parent; on an internal split, move the middle key up.
Recheck the parent after every promotion, since splits can cascade, and create a new root when the old root splits.
problemTypes.trap: Removing the separator from the leaf level in a B+ tree, or using a split rule different from the one the question states.

problemTypes.title: Classify an index as primary, clustering or secondary, dense or sparse
recipe: Ask whether the file is physically ordered on the index field: if yes, the index is primary (key field) or clustering (non-key field); if not, it is secondary.
Primary and clustering indexes can be sparse; a secondary index must be dense.
Remember the limits: at most one primary or clustering index per file, and any number of secondary indexes.
problemTypes.trap: Calling an index primary just because its field is a key; what matters is whether the file is sorted on that field.

problemTypes.title: Choose a file organisation or index for a workload
recipe: Equality lookups only: a hash index. Range conditions, ORDER BY or prefix searches: a B+ tree.
Many AND/OR conditions on low-cardinality columns in a read-mostly warehouse: bitmap indexes.
Insert-heavy data that is rarely searched, such as a log: a heap file.
problemTypes.trap: Choosing hashing for a range query, or a bitmap index for a frequently updated, high-cardinality column.

questions.stem: A file of 30,000 records, each 100 bytes, is stored unspanned in 1024-byte blocks and sorted on its key field. A primary index on that key uses 16-byte entries (a 10-byte key and a 6-byte block pointer). How many block accesses does a search for one record take using binary search on the index, including the access to the data block?
questions.explanation: The blocking factor is ⌊1024 / 100⌋ = 10, so the file has 30,000 / 10 = 3000 blocks. A primary index is sparse, with one entry per data block: 3000 entries. Each index block holds ⌊1024 / 16⌋ = 64 entries, so the index needs ⌈3000 / 64⌉ = 47 blocks. Binary search over them takes ⌈log₂ 47⌉ = 6 accesses, plus 1 for the data block: 7. Binary search on the data file alone would take ⌈log₂ 3000⌉ = 12.

questions.stem: A file of 30,000 records, each 100 bytes, is stored unspanned in 1024-byte blocks. A secondary index with 16-byte entries is built on a candidate key that the file is not sorted on, and it is then made into a multilevel index. How many block accesses does a search for one record take, including the access to the data block?
questions.explanation: A secondary index on a key is dense: 30,000 entries. At ⌊1024 / 16⌋ = 64 entries per block, the first level needs ⌈30,000 / 64⌉ = 469 blocks, the second ⌈469 / 64⌉ = 8 and the third 1. A search reads one block per level and then the data block: 3 + 1 = 4. Binary search on the 469-block first level alone would take ⌈log₂ 469⌉ + 1 = 10.

questions.stem: A B+ tree is stored in 1024-byte disk blocks. A search key takes 8 bytes and a child (block) pointer takes 4 bytes. What is the maximum number of keys an internal node can hold?
questions.explanation: An internal node with n keys has n + 1 child pointers, so 8n + 4(n + 1) ≤ 1024, which gives 12n ≤ 1020 and n ≤ 85. The node holds 85 keys and has 86 children; B+ tree internal nodes carry no record pointers.

questions.stem: B+ tree leaves are stored in 2048-byte blocks. Each leaf entry is a 10-byte key with a 6-byte record pointer, and each leaf also stores one 4-byte pointer to the next leaf. What is the maximum number of keys in a leaf?
questions.explanation: A leaf with n keys needs n(10 + 6) + 4 ≤ 2048 bytes, so 16n ≤ 2044 and n ≤ 127.75, which gives 127. Forgetting the next-leaf pointer gives 128, using the internal-node layout with 4-byte child pointers gives 146, and charging every key both pointers gives 102.

questions.stem: A B+ tree uses 1024-byte blocks, 8-byte keys, 4-byte block pointers and 4-byte record pointers. Internal nodes hold keys and child pointers; each leaf holds (key, record pointer) pairs and one pointer to the next leaf. What is the maximum number of keys a B+ tree with exactly 3 levels (root, one internal level, leaves) can index?
questions.explanation: Internal nodes: 8n + 4(n + 1) ≤ 1024 gives 85 keys, so up to 86 children. Leaves: 12n + 4 ≤ 1024 also gives 85 keys. A full root has 86 children, each of those has 86 leaf children, and each leaf holds 85 keys: 86 × 86 × 85 = 628,660.

questions.stem: In a B-tree of order m, where the order is the maximum number of children a node may have, what is the maximum number of keys in a node?
options: m
questions.explanation: A node with k keys separates k + 1 subtrees, so a node with at most m children holds at most m − 1 keys. ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 is the minimum for a node other than the root.

questions.stem: Every node of a B-tree can hold at most 7 keys. What is the minimum number of keys in a node other than the root?
questions.explanation: At most 7 keys means at most 8 children, so the order is 8. A non-root node needs at least ⌈8/2⌉ = 4 children and therefore at least 3 keys. Only the root may drop to a single key.

questions.stem: A B-tree has order 5: each node has at most 5 children. What is the minimum number of keys in such a B-tree with exactly 4 levels?
questions.explanation: Keep every node as empty as the rules allow. The root has 1 key and 2 children; every other node has ⌈5/2⌉ = 3 children and 2 keys. Levels 2, 3 and 4 then have 2, 6 and 18 nodes, so the tree holds 1 + 2·2 + 6·2 + 18·2 = 53 keys, which matches 2⌈m/2⌉^(L−1) − 1 = 2·27 − 1 = 53. Holding the root to the same minimum gives 80, rounding m/2 down gives 15, and 624 = 5⁴ − 1 is the maximum.

questions.stem: The keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 are inserted in this order into an empty B+ tree in which every node holds at most 3 keys. A leaf that overflows to 4 keys keeps its 2 smallest, moves the other 2 to a new right leaf and copies the smallest key of the new leaf into the parent. An internal node that overflows to 4 keys keeps its 2 smallest, moves the third up to its parent and puts the largest in a new right node. When the root splits, a new root is created above it. Which describes the final tree?
options: The root holds only 70; its two children hold [30, 50] and [90]
The root holds only 50; its two children hold [30] and [70, 90]
The root holds 40, 70 and 100, and the tree has two levels
The root holds only 90; its two children hold [30, 50, 70] and [100]
questions.explanation: Inserting 40 splits [10, 20, 30, 40] into [10, 20] and [30, 40] and copies 30 up. Inserting 60 splits [30, 40, 50, 60] and copies 50 up; inserting 80 splits [50, 60, 70, 80] and copies 70 up, so the root becomes [30, 50, 70]. Inserting 100 splits [70, 80, 90, 100] and copies 90 up, which overflows the root to [30, 50, 70, 90]. It keeps 30 and 50, moves 70 into a new root and puts 90 in a new right node. The leaves are [10, 20], [30, 40], [50, 60], [70, 80] and [90, 100], after four leaf splits and one internal split.

questions.stem: A file is physically sorted on dept_no, which is not a key: many records share each value. An index on dept_no has one entry per distinct dept_no, pointing to the first block that holds it. In the classification into primary, clustering and secondary indexes, what kind of index is this?
options: Primary index
Clustering index
Secondary index
Multilevel secondary index
questions.explanation: The file is ordered on the indexed field, so the index is primary or clustering, not secondary. A primary index needs the ordering field to be a key; dept_no repeats, so this is a clustering index. It has one entry per distinct value rather than one per record, and a file can have only one index of this kind.

questions.stem: A dense index has an entry for every search-key value in the file; a sparse index has entries for only some of them. Which statements are correct?
options: A sparse index can be built only on the field the data file is sorted on.
A secondary index must be dense.
On the same file and field, a dense index never needs more blocks than a sparse one.
Every index built on a key field is sparse.
questions.explanation: A sparse index finds the last entry not above the search key and scans forward from there, which works only if the file is sorted on that field. A secondary index is on a non-ordering field, so a value can sit in any block and every value needs an entry: it must be dense. A dense index has at least as many entries as a sparse one, so it usually needs more blocks. A secondary index on a candidate key is a dense index on a key field.

questions.stem: A B-tree and a B+ tree are built with the same block size, key size and pointer sizes. Which statements are correct?
options: Every search in the B+ tree ends at a leaf.
B+ tree internal nodes hold no record pointers, so they fit at least as many keys as B-tree nodes.
The B-tree stores each key twice, once in an internal node and once in a leaf.
Because B+ tree leaves are linked, a range query needs only one root-to-leaf search.
questions.explanation: In a B+ tree the record pointers live only in the leaves, so every search goes down to a leaf, and internal nodes, free of record pointers, have a higher fan-out. A range query finds its first key once and then follows the leaf links. It is the B+ tree that may hold a key twice, as a routing copy in an internal node; a B-tree stores each key exactly once.

questions.stem: Most queries on a table look like WHERE price BETWEEN 100 AND 200 ORDER BY price, and price has many distinct values. Which index on price suits these queries best?
options: A static hash index
An extendible hash index
A bitmap index
A B+ tree index
questions.explanation: A range condition with ordered output needs an index that keeps keys sorted. A B+ tree finds the leaf for 100 with one root-to-leaf search and follows the leaf links up to 200, returning keys in order. Hash indexes scatter neighbouring values across buckets and support only equality, and a bitmap index on a high-cardinality column needs one bit vector per distinct value.

questions.stem: An extendible hash file has global depth 3. An insertion overflows a bucket whose local depth is 2. The records in that bucket, together with the new one, do not all agree on the next bit of their hash values. What happens?
options: The directory doubles to 16 entries, and then the bucket splits
The record goes into an overflow chain, and nothing splits
The bucket splits into two buckets of local depth 3, which take over the 2 directory entries that pointed to it; the directory keeps 8 entries
Every bucket splits, and the global depth becomes 4
questions.explanation: A bucket of local depth 2 under global depth 3 is shared by 2^(3−2) = 2 directory entries. It can split on one more hash bit without new directory entries: the two halves get local depth 3 and one entry each. The directory doubles only when the overflowing bucket's local depth already equals the global depth.

questions.stem: In a B+ tree, an insertion overflows a leaf, which splits into two leaves. What happens to the separator key, the smallest key of the new right leaf?
options: It moves up to the parent and no longer appears in any leaf
It stays in the leaf level, and the parent does not change
It becomes the new root, whatever the height of the tree
A copy goes up to the parent, and the key stays in the new right leaf
questions.explanation: Every key must stay in the leaf level, where the record pointers live, so a leaf split copies the separator up and keeps the original in the right leaf. Only an internal-node split moves its middle key up out of the node. The promotion may cascade, and a new root appears only when the old root splits.

questions.stem: A file occupies b blocks. Which statements about block accesses are correct?
options: Inserting a record into a heap file takes O(1) block accesses.
Searching a sorted file on its ordering field takes about ⌈log₂ b⌉ block accesses.
A hashed file answers a range query on its hash key in O(1) block accesses.
Searching a heap file for a key value takes about log₂ b block accesses on average.
questions.explanation: A heap file appends to its last block, so insertion takes constant time, and a sorted file allows binary search over its blocks. Hashing scatters neighbouring keys across buckets, so a range query must scan the whole file. A heap file has no order, so finding a key reads b/2 blocks on average and b in the worst case.

pitfalls.text: A sparse index works only on the field the file is sorted on; an index on any other field must be dense.
A B-tree keeps record pointers in its internal nodes too, so its fan-out is lower than a B+ tree's internal fan-out for the same block size.
Hash indexes answer only equality searches; a range query or ORDER BY on the hash key still needs a full scan.
Bitmap indexes suit low-cardinality, read-mostly columns; on a high-cardinality or frequently updated column they are large and slow to maintain.
The ⌈m/2⌉ lower bound applies to every node except the root, which may have just 2 children and 1 key.
Check whether a question's order means the maximum number of children or of keys before using it; the two differ by one.
Count the final data-block access: an index search costs the index blocks read plus one data block.
A B+ tree leaf split copies its separator up, but an internal split moves its middle key up; mixing the two produces a wrong tree.

revisionCard.heading: File organisation
lines: Heap: insert O(1), key search b/2 blocks on average
Sorted: binary search ⌈log₂ b⌉; inserts must keep the order
Hashed: equality about 1 access, no range queries

revisionCard.heading: Indexes
lines: Primary: ordering key, sparse, one entry per block
Clustering: ordering non-key field; secondary: non-ordering field, dense

revisionCard.heading: B-trees and B+ trees
lines: Order m: non-root internal nodes have ⌈m/2⌉ to m children, the root 2 to m
B+ internal: nK + (n + 1)P ≤ B; leaf: n(K + Pr) + P ≤ B
B-tree, L levels: at most m^L − 1 keys, at least 2⌈m/2⌉^(L−1) − 1
Leaf split copies the separator up; internal split moves it up

revisionCard.heading: Hash and bitmap indexes
lines: Static: fixed buckets, degrades as the file grows
Extendible: directory doubles only when local depth = global depth
Linear: splits buckets in a fixed order, no directory
Bitmap: low cardinality, OLAP, fast AND/OR

errata.claim: Every internal node of an order-m B-tree has between ⌈m/2⌉ and m children, and between ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 and m − 1 keys.
errata.correction: The lower bounds hold for every node except the root, which may have as few as 2 children and 1 key, or no children at all when it is the only node. Without that exception a tree could never grow from one node to two levels.

errata.claim: A B+ tree of order p holds at most p keys per leaf and p + 1 children per internal node, and an internal node has between ⌈p/2⌉ and p children.
errata.correction: The two statements contradict each other. If the order p is the maximum number of keys, a non-root internal node has between ⌈(p + 1)/2⌉ and p + 1 children; if p is the maximum number of children, it has between ⌈p/2⌉ and p children and at most p − 1 keys. A question must fix one convention.

errata.claim: A secondary index is built on a non-key field.
errata.correction: A secondary index is built on any field the file is not ordered on, whether or not it is a key. On a candidate key it has one entry per record; on a non-key field it has either one entry per record or one entry per distinct value that leads to all matching records, often through an extra level of record-pointer blocks.

errata.claim: In extendible hashing the directory doubles on overflow.
errata.correction: It doubles only when the overflowing bucket's local depth equals the global depth. If the local depth is smaller, the bucket splits, its local depth grows by one and the directory entries that pointed to it are divided between the two halves, with no change in directory size.
